annotation.text: : child, shh, it is whispered. But when will someone tell me the full story? We buried
his house under cast-off sheetrock, beams, and broken appliances. Walk in my
flowering peony bed and you'll find it. A TV antenna made from a bent wire hanger.
What's left of Ralph Ellison's house. It picks up mysterious whispers.
Ars Poetica Number 100. I Believe. Poetry, I tell my students, is idiosyncratic.
Poetry is where we are ourselves, though Sterling Brown said, every eye is a
dramatic eye, digging in the clam flats for the shell that snaps, emptying the
proverbial pocketbook. Poetry is what you find in the dirt, in the corner, over here,
on the bus, God in the details, the only way to get from here to there. Poetry, and
now my voice is rising, is not all love, love, love, and I'm sorry the dog died.
Poetry, here I hear myself loudest, is the human voice. And are we not of
interest to each other? So now out of Ars, Poetica, just two more poems.
The dream that I told my mother-in-law. In the room almost filled with my, with,
again, in the room almost filled with our bed, the small bedroom, the king-size bed,
high up and on casters, so sometimes we would roll. In the room in the corner of
the corner apartment on top of a hill, so the bed would roll, we felt as if we
might break off and drift, float, become our own continent. When your mother first
entered our apartment, she went straight to that room and libated our bed with
water from your homeland. Soon she saw in my cheeks the fire and poppy stain, and
soon thereafter on that bed came the boy. Then months, then the morning I cracked,
first one, then two, then three eggs in a white bowl, and all had double yolks. And
your mother, now our mother, read the signs. Signs everywhere, signs rampant, a
season of signs and a vial of white dirt brought across three continents to the
enormous white bed that rolled, and now held three, and soon held four, four on
the bed, two boys, one man, and me, our mother reading all signs and blessing
our bed, blessing our bed filled with babies, blessing our bed through her
frailty, blessing us in our bed, blessing us in our bed. She began to dream of
childhood flowers, her long-gone parents. I told her my dream in a doctor's
waiting room. A photographer photographed women, said her portraits revealed their
truest selves. She snapped my picture, peeled back the paper, and there was my
son's face, my first son, myself. Mama loved that dream, so I told it again. And
soon she crossed over to her parents, sisters, one son. War took that son. We
destroyed one another, and women came by twos and tens, wrapped in her same fine
white, bearing huge pans of stew, round breads, homemade wines, and men came in
suits with their ravaged faces, and together they cried and cried and cried
and keened and cried, and the sound was alive, hives swelling and growing, all the
water in the world, all the salt, all the whales, and the sound grew too big for the
building, and finally lifted what needed to be lifted from the casket, and be
quieted, and watched it walk up and away, like feather, like ash. Daughter, she said,
when her journey began, you are a mother now, and you have to take care of the
The African Picnic. World Cup finals, France v. Brazil. We gather in Gideon's
yard and grill. The TV sits in the bright sunshine. We want Brazil, but Brazil won't
win. Aidan waves a desultory green and yellow flag from the east to the west, to the west
the east. We scatter and settle and scatter some more. Through the window,
mama watches from the pool indoors. Jonah scarfs meat off of everybody's plate,
kicks a basketball long, and hollers, bold, and roars like the mighty lion he is.
Baby is of Kasha, surrounded by pillows, in the bevy of Horn of Africa girls, who
coo like lovers, pronounce his wonders, oil and massage him, brush his hair. My
African family is having a picnic here in the USA. Who is here and who is not?
When will the phone ring from far away? Who in a few days will say goodbye? Who
will arrive with a package from home? Who will send presents in other people's
luggage and envelopes of money in other people's pockets? Other people's children
have become our children here at the African Picnic. In a parking lot, in a
taxi cab, in a winter coat, in an airport queue, at the INS, on the telephone, on
the crosstown bus, on a south side street, in a brand new car, in a jella-ba, with a
cardboard box, with a Samsonite, with an airmail post, with a bag of spice, at the
African Picnic, people come and go. The mailman sees us say goodbye and waves
with us. Goodbye, goodbye, as we throw popcorn, eulolate. Ten or twelve
suitcases stuffed in the car. Goodbye, mama, goodbye. The front door shut, the
driveway bare. Goodbye, mama, goodbye. The jet alights into the night, a huge metal
machine in flight. Goodbye, mama, goodbye. At the African Picnic, people come and go
: I was just thinking about what Sonia was saying about security. Remember when she was
talking about security? I was thinking, this room is a big security risk. Really big.
I'm going to read a few poems of despair and a few of love. I hope you can tell the difference.
My mother tried to do some historic research about our family. She searched public
documents and asked family members who still live in Beaumont, Texas, but Black
births weren't recorded until after the Emancipation Proclamation. So it seems our
family tree goes over a cliff if you go backwards. The first birth recorded was three years after
Philomene Durant, born in 1868, my great-grandmother. Before then, it's like we never existed. My
mother wrote to our Aunt Faye, the oldest living relative, for information about Philomene,
her grandmother, my great-grandmother, who was known as Mom. This was Aunt Faye's letter.
I just took the letter and broke it into lines. I left the spelling. I might say a parenthetical
remark just to clarify. Now, About Mom. I have never heard anything about these things
that has been told to you. Mom had her children, but did not raise them. When Lawrence, one
of her children, came to visit me, he went all over Beaumont to find a lady that he thought
a lots of. She had been good to him as a child in his young life. And he never talked about
Mom, Philomene. You see, Mom had more than one set of children. Clarence O. Jackson lived
with a family of Italian and spoke their language. They had a store. Lawrence's and your mother,
Regina, were Durants. Their father was a Frenchman. Then there was Rosa Gaud. Alice and Baptiste
were Gauds. The woman that raised Baptiste, he brought her to see me. Philomene had a temper,
would pick up anything to hit her children with. She worked hard here in Beaumont for a little
or nothing for Jews. She washed and ironed. When your mother and father separated, Mom, Philomene,
stayed with her son-in-law, your father, Mr. Joe. Your mother left a lots of things in the house that
Philomene treasured because they were her daughter's. I am sure why Mom's children never talked about
her life was because they had different fathers. About property, no mention anything about it. Mom's life
was not the best. She worked hard and she went to church. You know, she had what you call a milk leg,
a painful sore. She was ill. I went and got her and brought her home, taking care of that leg daily.
Your mother came and carried her to Louisiana to care for Alice, the darkest child, who had TB. Alice passed in
New Orleans March 13, 1941. She was with Sister Rosa. Alice, they called her Boots, was 29. Forget about the stories,
that's in the past about Mom.
I'm very interested in what our families didn't talk about and in the shadow that that

casts in our lives and in our own hearts. The Body Awakening. Each morning when I get up, I sit with the body. The clitoris feels dead hiding in my abdomen, the tightened muscles are at crossed purposes.
Whatever is not felt it in the clitoris is deflected, blocked in the body like staunched blood.
I know the center of creativity must come from that tender bud so circumscribed. A few weeks ago at a writer's conference, my whole body hurt
with feelings. The clitoris throbbed. I was extruded out of myself. But when I left that place, came back to my safe husband, the man who loves me and will stay with me no matter what.

I began to feel sheltered, separated from the most powerful feelings, and the clitoris too drew back. I questioned my marriage. I married my husband because he was a harbor, a safe place in which I could stop feeling.
What is more punished among the angry than anger, among the unsatisfied than desired, among the hate-filled than hate, among the frightened than fear? I wanted to be still.

Such a ringing clearness, such a transparency of soul, that most vulnerable and singing part. The clitoris, like the shyest girl, must not be approached directly, but as if being entreated to make herself known, as if being sung to on a balcony by one filled with love and desire.

It is the very deepest secret that must be loved. Now, instead of demanding that my body respond, terrified and angry if it doesn't, I talk to myself, relax, you don't have to do anything, I won't push or demand.
A determination lets go some wall of protection, skin the hood around the clitoris, some psychic box receives. I'm with myself, like being in the presence of one you deeply love.
I found the G-spot, its rubbery quarter of a dime behind the cervix. I touched it in squat position until I felt its blood thickening, its full leaf like the thick petal of the pocketbook plant.
This is the place that makes me feel as if my womb breaks open, flowers, the pillow the penis rests on. A lesbian friend says, a hand is good enough for me.
From this I learned, tenderness, I who have been so demanding of others, of myself, to show or prove. We survive on a thin balance, testing the universe for signs of love.

As yesterday, gardening, a brown unburied seed speckled with dirt and carved with its own particular face. I found the clitoris, that earthy bone. I rubbed myself along the roughened texture of a sheet.
I found the nerves at the small fingers length in the anus. I have to take myself tenderly in my hands. Listen, I have to let myself happen, hoping but not certain.

Apart let's go. I will not force others as I will not force myself. I learned to respond in fear. I stayed alive in fear. I beat a life out of myself, a life in which I made myself smile, charm, act loving.
I did this by thinking about the possible loss under everything I did, thinking that I already had lost everything, lost my life.

Once a great poet said to me, one day you'll stop sitting there smelling sweet. These indications are not to be gotten rid of. Every cinch in my beating, breathing, every awareness of the rivers of nerve is a song of myself.
My body is instructor, aching, or so laid back that I feel dead to myself. To hold all these parts in consciousness as if it were a small thing, my life.
I think with great love of that little seat of power and wisdom, the clitoris, how it can't be seen unless, like the face, you look at it in the mirror.
This tenderness does not make the world easy. It is another way to envision living with myself as a child of a vicious father, and that part always with me, the old enemy, my aim and direction.
To live with myself, to regulate the unseen. Nothing on earth will change but this.
And I'm hoping I can get a couple Telly poems in.
Somebody came up to me after the last reading and and said Telly lives! Telly lives! Telly is a fish.
And so there are a couple poems about Telly that I'm going to try to get in now.
And it starts with a quote from Lucille Clifton, flesh is the coat we unfasten and throw off.
Telly's favorite artist was Alice Neel.
When he came to my house, I propped up her bright yellow shade with open window and a vase of flowers, postcard size, behind his first fishbowl.
I thought it might give him something to look at, like a heart, the center of the house you keep coming back to, a root for your eye.
It was a wondering in me that came up with that thought, a kind of empathy across my air and through his water, maybe the first word that I'd propped up between us in case he could hear.
I put up others, but Neel was the only one he'd stare at for hours, hanging there with his glassy eyes wide open.
At night he wanted the bottom, as if it were a warm bed, he'd lie there, sort of dreaming, his eyes gray and dim and thoughtless.
For months he came back to her, the way a critic or lover can build a whole life on the long study of one great work.
I don't know why he stopped, maybe it was when he first noticed me, the face above my hand feeding
For sometimes when I'd set the food on top, he'd still watch me eye to eye,
As if saying, food isn't enough.
Once when I'd bent, he jumped up out of the water and kissed my lips.
What is a fish's kiss like?
You'd think it would be slimy, but it was quick, nippy, hard.
Maybe it was just what I expected, for all our fears of touch, it takes so long to learn how to take in.
When he stopped coming to the top, I guess I did all the wrong things.
The fish medicine, that smell, the codeine measured carefully for his ounce of weight.
For his gills worked so hard, and he lay still, tipped over slightly, like a dead boat.
How do you stop the hurt of having to breathe?
After, I took him to the middle of the yellow bridge, right near the Andy Warhol Museum.
I had put a paper towel in a painted egg and laid him in it, and at the top, I opened the casket and emptied him out into the water.
Because I was good to Telly in his life.
Because I taught him Alice Neel and fed him frozen mealworms until I found out that he'd lose his bright red tail color for that pleasure.
Because I paid $100 for a pet sitter to come when I was away on trips,
never liking those who said their betta did just fine sitting on the edge of their office desk over a long weekend.
How would you like not to eat for three days, I wanted to ask.
For choosing carefully among the pet sitters, interviewing, for looking for one who took a fish seriously,
and new betta stories of how smart they are, checking you out with a certain calm or anxious look in the eye.
Because I believed in Telly's worthiness for a funeral with elegant trappings.
Because I believed in one fish's brain and life and skill.
Because I put him in a painted wooden egg at the end and drove him down to the famous arching yellow bridge of Pittsburgh
and let him go into the frozen Monongahela, saying prayers for my lover or husband or brother of a year.
Because of this I am certain he sent me a gift from the China blue rivers of heaven.
A lovely man who first kissed me on that bridge, Kissing Bridge as he named it a few months later,
sending a photo after rain of Kissing Bridge underwater, scrawled with his loose sprawling letters.
Because all things are connected, a circle, bread on the water, as my mother said, always comes home.
: I just want to say a few things. Hi Marilyn! I'm so glad to see you. You're the only one that I hadn't spoken to yet.
So welcome to James Madison University and Furious Flower.
Well, we've had a feast. We've had more than a feast. Yes?
: Somebody's glasses are laying on the lip of the stage.
: Okay, so someone won't take those. Don't leave those.
I want to say just a couple of things.
This is the second pair he's lost.
I want to tell you just a couple of things.
The buses are available to take you back so you can revive yourselves and get ready to party.
And if you haven't heard, Sister Sonia has a CD.
And from what I've been told, I haven't heard the album it yet.
And I hear that Full Moon of Sonia is going to really kick it.
As my daughter used to say, what's the word now?
I don't know whether I can even lift this up.
But I know there's somebody out there who might even be able to dance in the aisles.
But I want you to do, well you know we may create a new paradigm here at JMU.
You know people in Harrisonburg, when they talk about a party, they talk about getting a glass of wine and getting some cheese, getting around, talking intellectual stuff.
I am so happy when I go someplace else and when they talk about a party, they talk about dancing.
So that's what we're prepared to have this evening.
I want you to have a great time.
And we've decided to take all of the books, all the bags, all the t-shirts to Wilson, where the concert is going to be.
So that you can do your last minute shopping.
I have decided that this is going on sale because they were kind of hidden.
And so I know a lot of people didn't see them, but those people who want this bag, instead of having this bag for $15, I think I'm going to reduce it to

Believe me, we did everything in the world to get this registration down.
Do you understand that our registration was $95?

And you know why we didn't include the bags in your registration package?

Toi Derricotte talked me into being on the board.

When you, Major Jackson, get your first real, real, real big book deal, I want you to give at least $10,000 to the Cave Canem.
: Major, I think you already won.
